div.p: Column 1 her. Primae litterae dubiae sunt. αὐτήν Jensen: om. Kenyon.When I told her what had happened, πραχθέντα Revillout: πεπραγμένα Diels.and that Athenogenes was harsh with me and unwilling to agree to anything reasonable, she said that he was always like that, but told me to take heart; for she herself would help me fight it out in everything.

And she said this while being as earnest in her manner as could be, and swearing the greatest oaths that she was truly speaking with goodwill toward me and with complete truth; so that I, gentlemen of the jury, for the truth shall be told ῥηθήσεται Jensen:εἰρήσεται Kenyon.to you, was persuaded of this. So, as it seems, love unsettles the nature of a man, ἀνθρώπου Blass: ἡμῶν τὴν Diels.when it has taken on a woman's assistance. συνεργίαν Jensen:ποικιλίαν Kenyon: alii alia.She at any rate, cheating me in all ἅπαντα Diels: τὰ μάταια Kenyon.these things, cut off for herself in addition, supposedly ὡς δὴ Diels: ἔτι Jensen.for a slave girl, three hundred drachmas, for the sake of her goodwill.

Perhaps, then, gentlemen of the jury, it is not very ὑπερθαύμαστόν ci. Kenyon, qui tamen οὕτω θαυμαστόν habet: tantumθαυμαστόν Jensen.surprising that I was led along in this way by Antigona, a woman who, as they say, among the courtesans of her time was the cleverest, and has continued διατετέλεκε Weil.to keep a brothel enhas ruined the house of the Cholleidian, which was inferior to none. οὐδενὸς ἐλάττω Jensen: οὐ φαῦλον οὕτω Blass.And yet when, by ὅπου καθʼin add. Jensen:ἥτις καθʼBlass:εἰ καθʼWeil.herself, she accomplished such things, what do you think τί οἴεσθʼ Kenyon.she has in mind ἐννοεῖν Jensen:ἐπιτελεῖν Weil.now, having taken on προσλαβοῦσανKenyon.as her partner Athenogenes, Column 2a man who is a speech-writer and a man of the market, and, most important of all, an Egyptian?

In the end, then, not to speak at length, for γάρ del. Kenyon.having sent for me again later she said that after spending many words on Athenogenes she had with difficulty persuaded him to release to me both Midas and his two sons for forty minas, and she told me to provide the money as quickly as possible, before Athenogenes should change his mind about anything.

So I collected it from every source, troubling my friends, and having deposited the forty minas at the bank I came to Antigona. And she gathered συνήγαγεν Revillout.us together in the same place, me and Athenogenes, and reconciled us, and urged us for the future to treat each other well. And I said I would do so, and Athenogenes here, taking up the word, said that I ought to be grateful to Antigona for what had been done; and now, he said, for her sake I will show you at once how much good I will do you. For γάρ Diels.you, he said, will pay down καταβαλεῖς Kenyon.the τὸ Diels.money for the freedom of τοῦWeil:τῇDiels.Midas Μίδου Revillout.and of the boys, but I will sell them to you by purchase and sale, so that, first, no one may molest παρενοχλῇ Blass: σε ἐνοχλῇ Revillout.or corrupt the boy, and then παῖδα, ἔπειτʼ Blass (secundum Jensen': Μίδαν, εἶτʼ Kenyon.that they themselves may not μὴ Blass.attempt to act wickedly πονηρεύεσθαι Weil.in any way because of their fear.φόβον Kenyon.

But Column 3the most important thing is this: as it is, they would seem to have become free through me; but if you buy them by purchase and sale and then later, whenever you see fit, set them free, they will owe you double gratitude. However, whatever money they owe, the price of some perfume to Pancalus and Procles, and anything else that any of the customers deposited at the perfume shop, as happens, these, he said, you will take over; but they are quite small, and there is much more stock than these in the workshop, perfume and alabaster jars and myrrh, and he named some other things, from which all these debts will be paid off διαλυθήσεται Weil.easily.

And here, gentlemen of the jury, as it seems, lay the plot and the great fabrication. For if I paid down the money for their freedom, I would lose only what I gave him, but I would suffer nothing terrible; but if I bought them by purchase and sale, having agreed with him to take over the debts, ἀναδέξεσθαι Blass:ἀναδέξασθαι P, ut vid. (sed littera a dubia), Kenyon, et in add. Jensen.as being worth nothing, because I did not know them beforehand, he would have caught the contributors to the loans too in the agreement; which is just what he did.

For when, after he had said this, I agreed, he at once took a document from his lap and read out the text that was written τι τὸ ἐγγ . . Blass: τὸ ἐγγ . . Kenyon: τι προγ . . Colin.in it. Column 4This was an agreement with me; I listened to it while it was being read, but I was eager to settle the business I had come for, and he seals the agreement at once in the same house, so that none of those well disposed to me should hear what was written in it, adding beside my name that of Nicon of Cephisia.

Going to the perfume shop, we deposit the document with Lysicles of Leuconoe, Λευκονοιεῖ Kenyon:Λευκονοεῖ P.and I paid down the forty minas and made the purchase. When this had happened, the creditors to whom money was owed by Midas came to me, and the contributors to the loans, and they talked with me; and within three months all the debts had become known, so that I owed, together with the loans, as I said just now, about five talents.

When I realized what trouble I was in, then at last I gathered my friends and relatives, and we read the copies of the agreement; in it the names of Pancalus and Polycles were written explicitly, and that prices for perfumes were owed, which were small, and about which they could say that the perfume in the workshop was worth the money; but most of the debts, and the largest, were not entered under Column 5names, but as a supplementary item, as though they were nothing: and if Midas owes anything to anyone else.

And of the loans, one, [Dicaeocrates], Δικαιοκράτης del. Weil.was entered, of which three instalments remained; this one was written under the name of Dicaeocrates; but the others, on the strength of which Midas had received εἰλήφει ὤφειλε Weil.everything, and they were newly raised, these he did not enter in the agreement, but concealed them.

When we deliberated, we decided to go to this man and talk with him. And finding him by the perfume stalls we asked him whether he was not ashamed of lying and of having ambushed us with the agreement, by not declaring the debts beforehand. He answered us that he neither knew of the debts we were talking about, nor paid any attention to us, and that he had a document deposited, concerning me, about these matters. As many people were gathering and listening to the affair, because the talk took place in the market, and were cutting him to pieces and urging us to arrest ἀπάγειν et sq. ad col. 6 finem plerumque restituit Blass.him summarily as a kidnapper, this we did not think ᾠόμεθα Weil: οἰόμεθα P.we ought to do, but we summoned him before you according to the law. First, then, he will read you the agreement; for from the actual ἐξ αὐτῶν Revillout.words Column 6written you will learn the plot of this very man. Read the agreement.

What was done, then, gentlemen of the jury, you have heard point by point. But Athenogenes will presently say to you that the law says that whatever agreements one man makes with another are binding. Just ones, at least, my good man; but those that are not, on the contrary, it forbids to be binding. And I will make this clearer to you from the laws themselves. For you have so disposed me and made me so afraid that I may be ruined by you and your cleverness, that I examine and study the laws night and day, making everything else a side matter.

The one law, then, orders that there be no lying in the market, ἀγορᾷ Revillout.laying down, I think, a command that is the finest of all; but you, lying in the middle of the market, had an agreement made against me. For if you show δείξῃςWeil.that you declared beforehand προειπὼν Revillout.to me the loans and the debts, or that you wrote in the agreement as many as I learned of, I have nothing ἐπυθόμην, οὐδὲνFuhr.to say against you, but I admit that I owe it.

And after this another law is about the matters in which, Column 7agreeing, περὶ ὧν Weil:ὁμολογοῦντες Revillout: κεῖται περὶ ὧν οἱ πωλοῦντες Volckmar.people make contracts with one another: whenever someone sells a slave, he must declare beforehand if it has any infirmity; if not, the slave may be returned. And yet where it is permitted to return a household slave if the seller does not disclose the diseases that come from fortune, how is it that you need not take responsibility for the wrongs contrived by you? Moreover, an epileptic slave does not also destroy the property of the buyer, but Midas, whom you sold me, has destroyed even that of my friends.

Consider, Athenogenes, how the laws stand not only concerning household slaves but also concerning free persons. For surely both you and all the οἱ add. Blass.others know that the children born of betrothed wives are legitimate. But indeed ἀλλὰ μὴνet sq. ad col. 8 finem plerumque restituit Revillout.it was not enough for the lawgiver that the woman be betrothed by her father or her brother, but he wrote expressly in the law: whatever woman a man betroths on just terms as his wife, from her the children are to be legitimate, εἶναι παῖδας γνησίουςWeil.and not καὶ οὐκ Blass: ἀλλ’ οὐκ Weil.if someone, falsely claiming her as his daughter, betroths some other woman. But the just ὡς θυγατέρα usque ad δικαίας Fuhr.betrothals as valid, and those not just as invalid, he establishes.κυρίαςusque adκαθίστησινBlass.

Further, the one about Column 8wills, too, is a law very similar to these; for it orders that one may γὰρ ἐξεῖναι Blass.dispose of one's own property however ὅπως ἄν Fuhr.one wishes, except on account of old age or disease or madness, or when persuaded by a woman, or overpowered by imprisonment or by necessity. But where not even concerning a man's own private property are unjust μὴ δίκαιαι Blass.wills valid, how can such terms be valid for Athenogenes, who made an agreement about κατὰ τῶν Kenyon.my property?

And if a man, as it seems, persuaded by his own wife, writes γράψῃ Diels.a will, it will be invalid; but if I was persuaded by the mistress of Athenogenes, must I με Weil.be ruined as well, I who have the greatest μεγίστην Weil.help, that written in the law, since I was compelled by these people to make this agreement? And then do you insist on the agreement which, having ambushed me, you and the mistress of yours ἑταίρα σουDiels.sealed, and on account of the very things for which the laws bid you be guilty of conspiracy, on these grounds do you claim to take something besides? ὑπὲρ ὧν usque ad ἀξιοῦτε Jensen in add.: alii alia.And it was not enough for you to have received the ἦν τὰςWeil.forty minas for the perfume shop, but also five talents you took away in addition προσαφείλουKenyon:ἀπεστερήκατεWeil. from me, as if hypo ὑποχείριον ἐν ποδοστράβῃ κατειλημμένον Revillout, coll. Harpocratione s.v. ποδοστράβη· ὑπὸ θηρευτοῦ κτλ. Richards.caught

s did not knowMidas adsthenta al Column 9 sinto the affairs of the market; but, quietly Coll. 9, 10, 11 plerumque restituit Blass. ἀτρεκὲς δὴ ἐγὼ Kenyon.biding my time, within three ἐν τρισὶ Weil.months I learned all the debts and the loans, while this man, who is a perfume-seller of three generations' standing, sitting in the market every day, owning three perfume shops besides, and every month receiving accounts, did not know the debts. In other matters he is no layman, but towards his slave he became so naive; and some of the debts, as it seems, he knew, but the others he says he does not know, whichever he does not wish to.

But such an argument of his, αὐτοῦ Revillout:οἶμαι Kenyon.gentlemen of the jury, is not a defence, ἀπολόγημά Reinach.but an admission that I need not pay the debts. For when he says that he did not know all ἅπαντα Revillout.the sums owed, surely he cannot say this, τόδʼ Kenyon.that he told me beforehand about the debts; and whatever I did not ὅσα δ’ οὐκ Revillout.hear from the seller, these I am not bound to pay. That you knew, Athenogenes, that Midas owed this money is, I think, evident to all, both from many other things and from your asking Nicon on my behalf as guarantor, ifthe debts being sufficientno. Certainly not Iby this argument of yours

Column 10If you, through not knowing, did not tell me μοι Diels.all the debts beforehand, and I made the agreement thinking that the debts were only those I heard of from you, which of the two ought to pay, the later purchaser or the one who long ago owned it, when the money was being borrowed? For I think it is you. But if indeed we dispute about this, let the law be our arbitrator, which was laid down not by lovers nor by those who plot against other people's property, but by the most democratic Solon;

who, knowing that many sales take place in the city, laid down a law that is just, as is agreed by everyone, that the damages which the slaves cause and their offences ἀδικήματα Jensen olim: ἀναλώματα Revillout.are to be made good by the master for whom the slaves happen to work. ἂν ἐργάσωνται Weil.Rightly so; for if any good ἐάν τι ἀγαθὸν Weil.is achieved or work found by the slave, to the owner it belongs. But you, disregarding the law, talk about agreements being broken. παραβαινομένων Diels.And while Solon thinks that not even what was justly proposed as a decree by anyone should, than the law, ψήφισμά τις τοῦ νόμου Jensen.be more authoritative, you, even σὺ δὲ καὶJensen:σὺ δὲ οἴει Blass.the unjust agreements, demand should prevail ἀξιοῖς κρατεῖνJensen:δεῖν κρατεῖνBlass.over all πάντωνRevillout.the laws.

And besides this, gentlemen of the jury, to my father and to my other friends he said thatethelas a gift Column 11 keand that, when he had told κελεύσας Jensen: κελεύοι με Weil.me to leave Midas to him and not buy him, I was unwilling and wanted to buy them all. And they say that he intends to say this to you as well, so that he may seem moderate, as if he were going to talk to some fools who will not notice this man's shamelessness.

But what happened you must hear; for it will be seen to be consistent with the rest of their plot. For the boy, whom just now I mentioned, he sent to me with the message that he would not stay with me unless I freed εἰ μὴ λύσομαι Kenyon: ἂν μὴ ὠνῶμαι Weil.his father and his brother. ἀδελφόν Weil.When I had already agreed to pay down for them, being three, the money, ἀργύριονRevillout.Athenogenes, going up to some τιναςDiels.of my friends

For my part, I think it was you two. Column 15 Having broken the common agreements of the city, he insists on his private ones with me, as if anyone would be persuaded that this man, who despised his obligations towards you, would have cared about those towards me; ἐμὲ Diels.he who is so wicked and everywhere the same that, even when he came to Troezen and the Troezenians made him a citizen, he fawned upon Mnesias the Argive and, appointed magistrate by him, expelled the citizens from the city, as they themselves will testify to you; for they are living here in exile.

And you, gentlemen of the jury, received them when they were banished, made them citizens and gave them a share in all your good things, remembering the service they did against the barbarian, after more than ἢKenyon.fifty and a hundred years, and thinking that it was right that those who had been useful to you in times of danger should, in their misfortune, be rescued περισωθῆναι Jensen in add.by you.
